newsitem.title: EGYPT: Yemeni opposition says election boycott spreading.
newsitem.headline: Yemeni opposition says election boycott spreading.

text.p: The leader of the Yemeni opposition in exile said a campaign to boycott next month's parliamentary elections was gaining ground and at least 80 percent of people would not vote in the south.

Abderrahman al-Jiffri, leader of the National Opposition Front (MOWJ), told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday night that the government had already fixed the elections through multiple registrations by army and security personnel.
The main internal opposition party, the Yemen Socialist Party (YSP), and at least two others have announced a boycott of the April 27 elections because of the alleged irregularities.

But Jiffri, who was vice-president of the short-lived secessionist southern state during the civil war of 1994, said support for a boycott was spreading to the Islah (Reform) Party, the junior partner in a ruling coalition with President Ali Abdullah Saleh's General People's Congress.
He said the branch of Islah in the large town of Taizz, a northern town close to the old border with the south, had announced a boycott and other branches might follow.
"Islah has 18 seats from Taizz in the last elections and it seems that the Congress wants to force Islah to choose certain weak people from Islah for these areas," he said.
"We think that if things continue like this, maybe the Ibb branch of Islah will follow, maybe Aden will follow, maybe Hadramwaut too," he added.
"The information we have received from the country is that people are ready to boycott...People are fed up now. In the south not less by any means than 80 percent (will not vote).
"We are sure of this in the south, although now they are trying to threaten the people that anybody who doesn't vote will be out of his job, he will never receive a salary," he said.

The MOWJ, which is mainly southern-based and which contains most of the YSP leaders in exile, has opposed the elections for months on the grounds that the government has failed to carry out promises to achieve national reconciliation with the south.
The southerners lost the 1984 war and the MOWJ says the Sanaa government has since treated the area as conquered territory, rather than an equal part of the country.
It says military commanders from the north run the south under martial law and discriminate against southerners.

"One side won the war and now they want to run one-sided elections. Ali Abdullah Saleh tried to implement a military solution to a political crisis in 1994 and now I think he will try a security and military solution for his own democracy. He will have to hold the elections by force," Jiffri said.

One of MOWJ's main complaints was over the registration process last year. Jiffri, who is on trial in his absence for his activities during the war, said the army moved its units around the constituencies during the registration period and registered soldiers in more than one area.

"Some people are listed in three or four places. They have even registered children," he said. A Western diplomat in Sanaa said the election was flawed, with 80,000 cases of double entries in voter registration.
Jiffri said that any foreign observers who go to monitor the elections should not concentrate on the mechanics of voting.
"We want them to come to watch the reaction of the people, to see how people feel, not to watch if the election is fair or not because it's already fixed," he said.
